The Yellow striped flounder Pseudopleuronectes herzensteini is a commercially significant pleuronectid inhabiting the coastal waters of northeastern Asia. Field surveys indicate that the maximum body length attained by this species reaches 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], positioning it as a moderately sized flatfish within its genus. However, the species exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in mass: ultimate female wet weight has been recorded at 1400 grams [Wwi = 1400 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships in fully grown adults. Growth trajectories appear to be influenced by the relatively cool waters of its habitat, where the onset of reproductive activity is delayed compared to more southerly distributed pleuronectids. The species is iteroparous, with spawning events occurring annually once maturity is attained.

At the onset of gonadal maturation, individuals first become reproductively viable upon reaching a total length at puberty of 20 cm [Lp = 20 cm]. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty has been calculated at 81.1 grams [Wwp = 81.1 grams], based on morphometric measurements taken from specimens undergoing initial gonad development. This length threshold represents a critical ecological milestone, as individuals below this size do not contribute to the breeding population. The relationship between body size and maturity is tightly linked to the annual thermal cycle, with gonadal recrudescence typically initiating during the late autumn cooling period. Juveniles and sub-adults below 20 cm [Lp = 20 cm] allocate somatic growth preferentially over reproductive investment, a pattern observed across many temperate flatfish species.

Embryonic development under controlled laboratory conditions proceeds most rapidly at a stable temperature of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C]. At this thermal regime, the age at birth, measured from egg fertilisation to larval eclosion, is 5.5 days [ab = 5.5 days] — a hatching time that is notably rapid compared to other pleuronectids incubated at similar temperatures, reflecting the minute egg diameter and the high metabolic rate characteristic of small teleost eggs at a temperature of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C]. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, with a wet weight at birth of 0.0000655 grams [Wwb = 0.0000655 grams], a value reflecting the minute egg diameter of approximately 0.5 mm reported for this species. These tiny prolarvae are endotrophic, relying entirely on their yolk reserves during the first days post-hatching. The rapid hatching time at 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C] is consistent with the relatively high metabolic rates expected for small, transparent teleost eggs incubated in cool-temperate waters.

Longevity data for Pseudopleuronectes herzensteini, compiled from extensive tag-recapture studies conducted in the Sea of Japan, indicate a life span of 5475 days [am = 5475 days] under natural conditions at a mean annual temperature of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C], a duration that places this species among the longer-lived flatfish relative to its maximum body size. Older individuals occasionally exhibit signs of reproductive senescence, with a decline in fecundity and egg quality observed in females beyond the age of 10 years. The relationship between temperature and longevity is well documented in this species: the lifespan estimate of 5475 days [am = 5475 days] is derived from populations experiencing the average thermal regime characteristic of its range, where summer and winter extremes are moderated by coastal currents at a temperature of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C].

Comparing the life-history strategy of this species with other members of the Pleuronectidae, the terminal body size and reproductive parameters suggest a moderate pace of life. The ultimate total length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm] corresponds well with asymptotic length estimates for congeneric species in the same thermal zone. Relatively large females can achieve a maximum body mass of approximately 1.4 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 1.4 kilograms], and these individuals are disproportionately important to population fecundity. The combination of a moderately extended lifespan and the capacity for large body size in females underscores the importance of protecting older age classes in fisheries management. Recruitment variability is closely tied to interannual temperature fluctuations, which affect both yolk-sac larval duration and the timing of the pelagic-benthic transition.
